analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare-participating hospitals and clinics from forcing nurses to work overtime beyond set limits, and protects nurses who refuse.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on August 6, 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no further action and no cosponsors outside three Democratic senators.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would use Medicare's rules as leverage: any hospital, surgery center, home health agency, or clinic that participates in Medicare could no longer require a nurse to work past a scheduled shift, beyond 48 hours in a week, beyond 12 hours in a row, or within 10 hours after a 12-hour shift, except during a declared emergency or disaster. Nurses could volunteer for extra hours, and they would gain whistleblower protection if they report violations, plus the right to sue nothing—instead, HHS could fine violating facilities up to $10,000 per violation and publish their names. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has seen no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses at Medicare-participating facilities gain enforceable limits on forced overtime, a guaranteed 10-hour rest after long shifts, whistleblower and anti-retaliation protections, and the backing of federal fines and public naming of violators. Patients benefit indirectly, since fatigue-driven medical errors are a documented patient-safety problem the bill's findings cite [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Providers that take Medicare could not force nurses to work more than a previously scheduled shift, more than 48 hours in a week, or more than 12 consecutive hours, nor could they force a nurse back on duty within 10 hours of a 12-hour shift.

The bill protects nurses from being fired, penalized, or reported to state licensing boards for refusing mandatory overtime or reporting violations, and lets them file complaints with HHS, which must investigate.

Providers face civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation (with higher penalties for repeat offenders), public posting of violators' names, and requirements to post notice and nurse schedules.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare-participating providers would bear the cost of filling staffing gaps with additional hires or voluntary overtime rather than mandatory overtime, plus paperwork, posting, and penalty exposure. Some of that cost could pass through to patients or insurers.

drawbacks.text: By capping mandatory overtime, the bill could force hospitals—especially rural or chronically understaffed ones—to either hire more nurses at significant cost or leave positions unfilled during a crunch, with no fallback short of a declared emergency.

The emergency exception only lifts the limits during formally declared disasters and does not cover everyday staffing crunches, so routine short-staffing (expressly excluded as 'consistent understaffing') would offer no relief route.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for nurse health and patient safety are well documented in the bill's own findings, and 18 states have already adopted similar limits, showing it is workable. The main costs fall on hospitals, which would have to hire more staff or restructure scheduling rather than rely on forced overtime, and the emergency exception is narrow enough that rural or understaffed facilities could face real strain. The bill does not address the underlying understaffing that drives overtime in the first place, but it targets the most dangerous symptom of it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, where no vote or further action has been taken; the Congress ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on August 6, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
No further action has been recorded since the referral—no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
The bill would attach a mandatory-overtime limit to Medicare participation, the main lever Congress has over most hospitals and clinics.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: If the bill dies in committee, hospitals and other providers keep their ability to require nurses to work overtime beyond scheduled shifts; nurses and patients gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Providers, so far — no action taken

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee where it has drawn no further action.

industries.industry: Hospitals and other Medicare-enrolled health care providers
industries.note: Hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, home health agencies, clinics, and similar providers lose the ability to fill staffing gaps by forcing nurses into overtime, which for many means hiring more staff or paying voluntary overtime rates. Emergency exceptions and a one-year lead time soften the burden.

industries.industry: Nurses (registered, licensed practical, and licensed vocational)
industries.note: Nurses gain enforceable limits on forced overtime, whistleblower and anti-retaliation protections, and the right to a 10-hour rest period after long shifts.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no Republican support and about two months left in the Congress. Bills at this stage—with no hearing or markup scheduled and narrow partisan sponsorship—almost never reach the floor. It is very likely to die in committee when the 119th Congress ends.
